topic: Family roles in consent with minors
stem: A consultant begins working with Sina, a 15-year-old soccer player whose family moved to the United States two years ago. At the first meeting, Sina's father explains that in their family important decisions are made together, and he expects to sit in on every session; he adds that he is not comfortable with Sina meeting alone with a new adult until he understands the work. The consultant usually meets minors one-on-one under a confidentiality agreement. Sina says little and glances at her father before answering. What is the most appropriate way for the consultant to proceed?
options: Review the usual one-on-one confidentiality agreement with both of them, then ask the father to approve it
Accept the father's presence as a family norm, and plan joint sessions with notes shared with both of them
Ask Sina and her father how each sees the family's role, then agree on how he will take part
Speak with Sina alone for a few minutes first to learn privately whether she wants her father in sessions
rationales: Walking the family through the standard agreement and seeking approval treats the consultant's default format as the starting point instead of learning how this family makes decisions; it invites a yes-or-no standoff rather than a negotiated arrangement.
Honoring the family's norm is well meant, but assuming it settles the question skips Sina's assent and her voice, and sharing all notes with both sets confidentiality limits without asking her.

Best. Culturally responsive consent with a minor combines guardian permission with the minor's assent. Asking both how they see the family's role, rather than assuming, lets the consultant negotiate an arrangement (for example, the father joins parts of sessions) with clear, agreed confidentiality limits.

Hearing Sina privately matters eventually, but the father has just said he is not comfortable with her meeting alone with a new adult; separating them at the first meeting overrides the guardian's permission before any arrangement is agreed.
takeaway: When a family's norms differ from your default format, ask how they see roles and negotiate consent that honors both guardian permission and the minor's assent.

stem: A city fire department contracts a consultant, who has worked only with college athletes, to offer performance and stress-management support to its crews. At the first station visit, several firefighters joke about 'the shrink from campus,' and a captain says outsiders 'never get how things work here.' The chief offers to make attendance at the consultant's sessions mandatory. What should the consultant do first to build credibility and rapport?
options: Spend shift time at the stations learning the crews' routines and norms, and ask what would help them
Open with a short briefing on firefighter stress research, and explain how the services were chosen
Accept required attendance for one introductory session, then keep all later sessions voluntary
Invite the captain to co-lead the first session so the crews see a respected insider backing the work
rationales: Best. Contextual intelligence means understanding an organization's culture, unwritten rules, and power structures before intervening. Learning the crews' world on their terms and asking what would help signals respect and builds the credibility an outsider lacks.
Evidence matters, but leading with research answers a question the crews have not asked and reinforces the image of an outsider who does not know how things work at the station.
Limiting the mandate to one session softens it, but it still ties the consultant to the chief's authority before any rapport with the crews exists and undercuts voluntary engagement from the start.
Borrowing a skeptical captain's endorsement before the consultant understands the culture is premature; it can read as a top-down push and asks the captain to vouch for work he has not yet seen.
takeaway: Entering a new culture, learn its norms and ask what is needed before offering expertise.

stem: Valeria, a professional volleyball player who recently joined a club abroad, has limited proficiency in the local language and asks to meet with the club's consultant about her worries over playing time and her relationship with the head coach. The club suggests that its bilingual assistant coach, who helps with lineup decisions, interpret the sessions. Her only bilingual teammate plays the same position she does. How should the consultant arrange communication for these sessions?
options: Use the assistant coach, after he signs a confidentiality agreement that covers everything said in sessions
Use the club's staff interpreter, who also interprets for the coaches in team and contract meetings
With Valeria's agreement, ask her bilingual teammate to interpret under a confidentiality pledge
Arrange a trained interpreter from outside the club who is bound by confidentiality and acceptable to her
rationales: A signed agreement does not remove the dual role: the assistant coach influences lineups, so his presence still makes candor about playing time and the head coach unlikely.

Professional training helps accuracy, but an interpreter who works for the club alongside the coaches, including in team and contract meetings, carries a dual role that makes candor about playing time and the head coach unlikely.

Her teammate competes with her for the same position and is not a trained interpreter, so this arrangement creates a dual relationship that compromises both confidentiality and accuracy, even with Valeria's agreement.

Best. A trained interpreter with no role in team decisions, who is bound by confidentiality and agreed to by the client, protects both accurate communication and the confidentiality boundaries of the relationship.
takeaway: Interpreters should be trained, independent of decision-makers, bound by confidentiality, and acceptable to the client.

stem: Before a training camp, a consultant plans to give a national goalball squad a brief questionnaire on pre-competition anxiety. All the players have visual impairments, ranging from partial sight to no light perception, and they variously use braille, screen readers, and large print in daily life. The assistant coach, who helps with selection, offers to help with administration. How should the consultant administer the questionnaire?
options: Read the items aloud to the squad as a group, and have each player give a rating in turn
Have the assistant coach read the items to each player one-on-one, and record each answer for them
Ask each player which format they use, and offer accessible versions they can complete privately
Email screen-reader-compatible versions to every player, and ask them to return the forms before camp
rationales: Reading items aloud keeps wording standard, but answering in front of teammates removes privacy and invites socially desirable answers about anxiety.
Individual administration helps access, but a staff member involved in selection hearing and recording each answer compromises confidentiality and makes candid reports of anxiety unlikely.

Best. Assessment should be administered in a way that fits each person's access needs while keeping the item content standard and responses confidential. Asking each player rather than assuming, then offering braille, screen-reader, or large-print versions completed privately, respects dignity and protects the validity of the answers.

A digital version is private and accessible for some, but it assumes everyone uses a screen reader when the squad uses a mix of braille, screen readers, and large print; the format should fit each player.
takeaway: Accommodate assessment administration to each person's access needs, by asking rather than assuming, while keeping item content standard and responses private.

stem: During an intake session in the middle of the competitive season, Idris, a collegiate 10,000-meter runner, mentions that he is fasting from dawn to sunset for Ramadan and has felt flat during afternoon workouts. His coach referred him, asking the consultant to 'find out why his motivation has dropped.' What should the consultant do next?
options: With his permission, ask the coach about moving his hardest workouts to the hours after sunset
Continue with the planned motivation inventory, since motivation is the coach's referral question
Refer him to the team dietitian for fueling guidance, and check in on his energy next week
Ask Idris how he observes the fast, what it means to him, and how he wants training handled
rationales: Rescheduling may become part of the plan, but proposing a solution to the coach before learning how Idris observes the fast and what he wants is premature and assumes what would help.
Staying with the coach's framing risks missing the contextual factor the athlete has just raised, and an inventory cannot capture what the fast means to him or how it shapes his training.
A dietitian may be useful later, with his agreement, but referring him on before exploring his observance and preferences treats the fast as a nutrition problem the consultant has not yet understood.

Best. Culturally responsive assessment explores the practice from the client's perspective rather than assuming its meaning or impact. Understanding his observance and preferences comes before any planning or, with his consent, coordination with the coach or other staff.
takeaway: When a client names a cultural or religious practice, ask what it means to them before interpreting its effect on performance.

stem: Terrence, a first-year rugby player, was referred because his tackling has become hesitant and he has missed several early-morning lifts. The consultant's intake form focuses on performance history and mental skills. Near the end of the session, Terrence mentions that he is the first in his family to attend college, works late shifts at a warehouse, and sends part of his pay home. How should the consultant proceed with the assessment?
options: Record these details, and finish the performance-focused intake before deciding whether they matter
With his consent, connect him to the campus first-generation program and the financial aid office
Widen the assessment to cover his work schedule, family obligations, and adjustment to college
Ask his strength coach whether the morning lifts could move to fit around his late warehouse shifts
rationales: Noting the details but deferring them treats his context as secondary; the late shifts and family obligations are likely explanations for the very problems in the referral.
Campus resources might help later, but the question is how to complete the assessment; connecting him elsewhere before understanding his situation is premature.

Best. Initial assessment should include cultural and contextual factors inside and outside the performance environment. Work demands, family obligations, and being a first-generation student may shape his fatigue, focus, and stress, and their meaning to him matters.
Problem-solving the schedule with a coach is an intervention, not assessment, and raising his work situation with staff before he has agreed to share it risks his confidentiality.
takeaway: Assessment covers the athlete's whole context; life outside sport often explains performance changes.

stem: In a first meeting, Theo, a professional contemporary dancer, says he is gay and asks whether the consultant has worked with LGBTQ+ performers, adding that past providers 'didn't get it.' The consultant has little experience with LGBTQ+ clients but solid experience with performance anxiety, which is Theo's presenting concern. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Be candid about the limited experience, ask what he needs, and decide together whether to proceed
Describe the consultant's track record with performance anxiety, and explain how it fits his goals
Acknowledge the gap, and ask whether he would like names of consultants who focus on LGBTQ+ clients
Thank him for raising it, and commit to completing LGBTQ+-affirming training before the next session
rationales: Best. Judging consultant–client fit is part of assessment. Transparency about experience, curiosity about what 'getting it' means to the client, and a shared decision reflect cultural humility and respect his autonomy.
Highlighting competence with his presenting concern is relevant, but it sidesteps the identity question he asked directly, echoing the providers he said 'didn't get it.'
Honesty about the gap is right, but moving straight to other names steers him toward a handoff before learning what he needs; his presenting concern is within the consultant's competence.
Further training is a reasonable longer-term step, but promising it centers the consultant's plan and still leaves unasked what 'getting it' means to Theo and whether the fit works for him now.
takeaway: When a client asks about your experience with their identity, answer honestly and decide fit together.

stem: A consultant observes a visiting national field hockey team at a training camp and interviews each player briefly. Most players give short answers, defer to the captain, and rarely make eye contact. The consultant's draft summary describes the squad as 'low in confidence with poor communication skills.' The team's liaison mentions that the consultant's interview style differs from how the players usually talk with staff. What should the consultant do before finalizing the summary?
options: Add the consultant's usual confidence questionnaire, and use it to confirm or revise the summary
Hold the labels as hypotheses, and check with the liaison what these behaviors usually signal
Re-interview the players in small groups, where they may speak more freely than one-on-one
Ask the captain to rate each teammate's confidence and communication to corroborate the draft
rationales: Adding a measure sounds multi-method, but the usual questionnaire may not be validated for this group, and it tests the consultant's interpretation without checking what the observed behaviors mean in context.

Best. Eye contact, brevity, and deference carry different meanings across cultural contexts. Culturally responsive assessment treats observations as tentative and checks them with cultural informants and the clients themselves before drawing conclusions.

A different interview format may help later, but it still filters responses through the consultant's own frame for 'confidence' and 'communication' rather than checking what the behaviors mean to this team.
Rating teammates asks the captain to apply the consultant's unexamined labels and puts a peer in an evaluative role, so it corroborates the interpretation rather than testing it.
takeaway: Read observed behavior through the client's cultural norms; check interpretations before labeling deficits.

stem: A consultant's standard intake form asks for 'mother's name' and 'father's name' and lists only two gender options. At an intake, Maren, a 24-year-old competitive climber, writes in that she was raised by her grandmother and leaves the gender item blank, later remarking that forms like this make her feel she has to explain herself. The consultant wants intake information that reflects each client's actual support system and identity. How should the consultant revise the intake process?
options: Add more checkbox options for family structures and gender, so that most clients find a category
Replace fixed categories with open fields in the client's words, and ask about key support people
Drop family and gender questions from the form, and raise them only if a client brings them up
Keep the form for consistency, and tell clients at intake that they may skip items that do not fit
rationales: More categories help, but any fixed list still leaves some clients outside it and asks them to fit the consultant's options rather than describe themselves.

Best. Culturally responsive assessment lets clients describe identity and family in their own terms. Open, self-described fields and questions about who actually supports them capture accurate context without assuming a family structure or gender.
Removing the questions avoids discomfort but discards context that matters for assessment and planning, and waiting for clients to raise it puts the burden on them.
Permission to skip items keeps the assumptions built into the form, so clients like Maren still meet categories that exclude them and must decide whether to explain themselves.
takeaway: Intake materials should let clients describe identity and support systems in their own terms rather than fit preset categories.

stem: During goal setting, Leilani, a collegiate softball pitcher, says she is uncomfortable with goals that feel 'all about me.' What drives her, she explains, is contributing to her team and making her family and home community proud. The consultant's usual template asks athletes to list personal outcome, performance, and process goals. How should the consultant approach the goal-setting plan?
options: Keep the standard template, and explain how personal process goals also end up serving the team
Set team performance and process goals with the coach, and fold her targets into the team plan
Start with a values-clarification exercise, and return to goal setting once her values are clearer
Frame her own performance and process goals around the team contributions and people she named
rationales: Explaining the template's benefits still overrides what she has said motivates her; goals framed in a way the athlete does not own are unlikely to build commitment.
Team goals have a place, but folding her into a team plan shifts an individual planning task to the team level and dilutes the controllable targets she can own.
Values work can be useful, but she has already named what drives her; delaying goal setting adds a step the situation does not require.

Best. Collaborative goal setting keeps the evidence-based structure (controllable performance and process goals) while framing it in the athlete's own values, which increases ownership and commitment.
takeaway: Adapt how goals are framed to the client's values; keep the evidence-based structure.

stem: A community youth soccer league asks a consultant to design a season-long mental skills program for players aged 10 to 13 and their families. In assessment interviews, coaches report that many parents work evenings and weekends, few families have reliable transportation or home internet, and many households speak Spanish or Vietnamese at home. Which planning decision best addresses these resources and barriers?
options: Invite families to weekend workshops at the league's main field, with interpreters and childcare
Build sessions into existing practices, and co-design translated family materials with parents
Offer brief video modules in Spanish and Vietnamese that families can watch on their own schedule
Train coaches to deliver the skills at practice, and send home family handouts prepared in English
rationales: Interpreters and childcare address language and caregiving, but weekend sessions at a central site still collide with weekend work and limited transportation.

Best. Planning should use the assessment's resources and barriers: practices already bring players together, and co-designing materials in families' home languages with parent representatives builds access, relevance, and buy-in.
Home-language videos ease scheduling and language, but they depend on the home internet access many families lack, and families have no voice in the design.
Embedding skills in practice uses an existing resource, but English-only handouts leave the language barrier unaddressed for many households.
takeaway: Design programs around the community's real barriers and involve its members in the design.

stem: Rafael, a 31-year-old national-team kayaker, plans to retire after the world championships in 18 months. He wants to stay fully focused on racing and asks to leave any talk about life after sport until his final race is over; he has already declined a meeting with his program's career advisor for the same reason. He has trained full time since age 19, has no other work experience, and says he 'can't picture' a life without paddling. How should the consultant approach planning for his transition?
options: Explore his worry about distraction, and discuss how small planning steps could fit his season
Agree to his request, and book a transition-planning session for the week after the championships
Encourage him to meet the program's career advisor now, while sessions stay centered on racing
Give him an athletic identity measure now, and use his scores to show why planning should start
rationales: Best. Planned, gradual transitions with pre-retirement planning and a broader identity are associated with better adjustment, and such planning need not hurt performance. Exploring his concern and discussing small steps respects his autonomy while giving him the evidence to decide.
Honoring his request without discussion leaves an athlete with an exclusive sport identity and no other work experience heading toward an abrupt transition, a known risk for difficult adjustment.
The advisor may well be part of his support, but he has already declined for fear of distraction; pressing the referral without exploring that concern is unlikely to work and fragments the plan.
Assessment can inform planning, but using scores to argue him into it turns a measure into a persuasion tool and skips the concern about distraction that is driving his request.
takeaway: Pre-retirement planning can start well before the final race and supports adjustment without costing performance.

topic: Responding to a microaggression in a workshop
stem: During a team-building workshop with a collegiate women's basketball team, a player asks a U.S.-born teammate of Korean descent, 'But where are you really from?' A few players laugh, and the teammate goes quiet and looks down. Earlier in the workshop, the team agreed on norms of respect and speaking up. How should the consultant respond?
options: Restate the team's respect norms in general terms, without singling anyone out, and move on
Continue the activity, then talk privately with the player who asked the question after the session
Briefly name the comment's impact, tie it to the agreed norms, and check in with the teammate later
Pause the activity, and invite the group to discuss how questions like that one can land for others
rationales: A general reminder avoids embarrassment, but without naming what happened the group cannot connect the norm to the comment, and the targeted athlete is left unsupported.
Private feedback to the speaker has a place, but the whole group saw the moment; leaving it unaddressed in the room signals that the agreed norms are not upheld and offers the teammate no support.

Best. The question conveys that she is a perpetual foreigner, a classic microaggression. Naming its impact briefly and without shaming, tied to norms the team set, protects psychological safety, and a private check-in supports the athlete who was targeted.
An open group discussion in the moment puts the targeted teammate on display and can pressure her to speak for the group; a brief, norm-based response is safer here.
takeaway: Address microaggressions promptly and briefly, anchored in group norms, and follow up with the person affected.

stem: A consultant is delivering a breath-focused mindfulness program to a police academy class to help recruits manage stress during scenario training. Two recruits tell the consultant privately that mindfulness feels to them like a religious practice that conflicts with their own faith. The consultant has already explained how the program is taught, and they remain uneasy about taking part. The academy director wants every recruit to complete the stress-management training. What is the most appropriate way to proceed?
options: Restate the research supporting the program, and invite them to try a single session before deciding
Let them observe sessions without taking part, and give them written materials on stress afterward
With their consent, connect them with the academy chaplain to talk through how the practice fits their faith
Ask about their specific concerns, and teach an alternative attention exercise with the same aim
rationales: They have already heard how the program works; pressing the evidence again treats their values as an information gap and pressures them to act against their stated beliefs.
Observing keeps them in the room but means they do not practice the skill, which falls short of the director's aim that every recruit complete the training.
A chaplain may be a support for them, but it turns a technique-fit question into a religious one outside the consultant's role and does not get them the stress-management skill.

Best. Respecting clients' rights and dignity means hearing their concerns and adapting the method, not the goal. An alternative attention-control or arousal-regulation exercise can build the same skill without asking them to act against their beliefs, and without the consultant ruling on whether the practice is religious.
takeaway: When a method conflicts with a client's beliefs, keep the goal and adapt the technique.

topic: Adapting imagery for a blind athlete
stem: A consultant begins imagery training with Amara, an elite para judoka who has been blind since birth. The consultant's standard scripts rely heavily on visual descriptions, such as seeing the opponent's stance and the arena lights. Amara is enthusiastic about imagery but says the first script 'didn't really land.' What should the consultant do next?
options: Rewrite the script around touch and sound cues drawn from published judo imagery guides
Ask Amara how grips, movement, and sound feel in her matches, and build scripts from her account
Move to self-talk and goal setting for now, and revisit imagery once her program is established
Have her coach describe how an ideal throw feels, and use that description to rewrite the script
rationales: Shifting to non-visual senses is the right direction, but generic cues from guides still assume how she experiences judo instead of drawing on her own sensory experience.

Best. Effective imagery reflects the performer's real sensory experience (the PETTLEP idea of functional equivalence). Asking how she experiences judo, rather than assuming, lets the consultant build kinesthetic, tactile, and auditory scripts that fit her.
Setting imagery aside delays a tool she is enthusiastic about when the problem is the script, not the technique.
A coach's description is secondhand and leaves Amara out of designing her own imagery; her experience, not someone else's, should shape the script.
takeaway: Adapt techniques to how the client actually experiences performance; ask, don't assume.

stem: At the end of a season with a professional women's soccer team, a consultant collects program evaluation forms that players complete with their names on them. Every rating is at the top of the scale. Several players who joined from clubs abroad later mention informally that, in those clubs, criticizing staff was considered disrespectful. How should the consultant interpret and follow up on this evaluation?
options: Treat the ratings as weak evidence, and gather anonymous feedback before drawing conclusions
Hold brief one-on-one interviews with each player, and ask what the program could do better
Compare the ratings with performance and attendance data, and report the combined findings
Report the ratings as preliminary, and repeat the same form at midseason to confirm the trend
rationales: Best. Named forms, power differences, and some players' norms against criticizing staff all push ratings upward, so uniform top scores are weak evidence for everyone, not just one group. Anonymous or peer-facilitated methods make candid feedback culturally and practically safer.
Interviews add depth, but face-to-face with the consultant whose work is being evaluated, players face the same pressure that produced the uniform ratings.
Outcome data can complement ratings, but performance and attendance reflect many influences, and this step leaves the candor problem with the ratings unaddressed.
Labeling the results preliminary is honest, but repeating the same named format reproduces the pressure toward positive ratings.
takeaway: Design evaluation methods that make honest feedback safe across cultural norms and power differences.

stem: A consultant employed by a professional hockey club has worked for a season with Jonas, a 27-year-old forward. The club tells Jonas his contract will not be renewed; he stays on the roster for two more weeks, and the consultant's role covers only rostered players. Jonas is shaken, says hockey is 'all I've ever been,' and is unsure whether to keep playing elsewhere. How should the consultant handle the end of this consultation?
options: Explore his options in the remaining sessions, and keep meeting informally once he leaves the roster
Prepare him for tryouts in the remaining sessions, since he has not ruled out playing elsewhere
Plan a closing session to review his gains, and connect him with ongoing transition support
Refer him to a licensed counselor now, since his distress after deselection signals a clinical need
rationales: Exploring options is useful, but continuing informally after his roster spot ends works outside the role the club contracts and blurs boundaries; any continued work needs a clear, separate arrangement.
He is unsure whether to keep playing, so focusing on tryouts decides his career question for him and reinforces an exclusive identity rather than supporting his own choice.

Best. Deselection is an involuntary transition that is especially hard when athletic identity is strong. A planned closing session consolidates what he has learned, and linking him to transition support (such as player-association programs or independent consulting) ensures continuity of care; a counseling referral becomes appropriate if his distress deepens or persists.
Being shaken by deselection is an expected reaction, not by itself a sign of a clinical concern; an immediate referral pathologizes his response and skips a planned ending.
takeaway: Conclude consultation deliberately, especially after an involuntary transition: review gains and connect the client to ongoing support.

topic: Revising a plan for acculturation stress
stem: Six weeks into a plan focused on pre-shot routines, a consultant reassesses progress with Ji-woo, a first-year collegiate golfer who moved from overseas for school. Her routine is consistent in practice, but her tournament scores have not improved. In the review, she describes feeling isolated, struggling with coursework in her second language, and rarely talking with teammates outside practice. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Add pressure-simulation reps to the routine work so it transfers from practice to tournament play
Connect her with the international student office, and keep the routine plan as written for now
Replace the routine work with adjustment support, and agree with her on when to resume it
Revise the plan with her to add adjustment and connection goals alongside the routine work
rationales: Pressure training targets transfer of a skill that is already consistent and ignores the barriers the reassessment just revealed.
Campus resources can help, but leaving the plan unchanged disregards the new reassessment data; evaluation exists to revise the plan when the picture changes.
Shelving the routine work overcorrects, even if the timing is agreed with her: her skill work is progressing, and adjustment support can run alongside it rather than replace it.

Best. Reassessment showed that acculturation stress and limited social support are likely barriers. Revising the plan collaboratively, for example by building connection with teammates and linking her to campus resources such as international student services and academic support, responds to the data while continuing the skill work.
takeaway: When reassessment reveals contextual barriers, revise the plan with the client rather than doubling down on the original skill.

stem: After attending a workshop on Latino cultural values, a consultant opens a first session with Andrés, a collegiate baseball player, by saying, 'I know family comes first in Latino culture, so let's start with your family's expectations.' Andrés looks puzzled and says his main concern is handling pressure at the plate. Which practice would best reflect cultural humility in this situation?
options: Explore family expectations gently, since they may still be shaping the pressure he feels at the plate
Use group knowledge only as a hypothesis, and let Andrés say what his background means to him
Pursue further training on Latino athletes so future sessions apply cultural research more precisely
Acknowledge the misstep, focus on his pressure concern, and leave cultural topics for him to raise
rationales: Family may matter, but pursuing it after he has named a different concern keeps the workshop's generalization in charge of the session; that is stereotyping, however gentle.

Best. Cultural humility is an other-oriented stance in which the client is the expert on their own identities, paired with ongoing self-reflection. Knowledge about groups is useful only as a tentative hypothesis checked with the individual.
More group knowledge reflects a mastery view of cultural competence; no amount of it lets a consultant predict an individual's values.
Owning the misstep and following his concern are good, but leaving culture entirely to him swings toward avoidance; humility means inviting his own view of what matters, not waiting.
takeaway: Cultural humility treats group knowledge as a hypothesis and the client as the expert on their own identity.

stem: A consultant is growing frustrated with Dante, a 19-year-old amateur boxer who often cancels sessions because his shifts at a delivery job change weekly. In her notes, the consultant writes that Dante 'doesn't seem committed.' Dante has said he wants to continue and asked whether sessions could be more flexible. She recalls that, as a college athlete, she never had to work during her season. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Examine how her own background shapes this judgment, and offer scheduling that fits his work
Give Dante a motivation inventory to test whether his commitment is as low as her notes suggest
Take her frustration to supervision, and plan strategies there for raising his commitment
Discuss the cancellations with Dante, and agree on an attendance standard he can commit to
rationales: Best. Self-reflexive cultural praxis asks consultants to examine how their own identities and privileges shape their interpretations. Her 'not committed' label may reflect her own experience rather than his, and supervision can support that reflection; flexible scheduling addresses the real barrier he has named.
Measuring his motivation treats her untested label as the question to answer, when the cancellations follow a structural constraint he has already described.
Supervision is the right venue, but going in to plan how to raise his commitment carries her assumption into the conversation instead of examining it.
Talking with him is collaborative, but an attendance standard treats a changing work schedule as a commitment problem and ignores the flexibility he asked for.
takeaway: When frustrated with a client, check whether your own background is shaping the interpretation.

topic: Extending competence for a Deaf client
stem: Nia, a collegiate wrestler who is Deaf and communicates primarily in American Sign Language, asks to work with the athletic department's consultant on pre-match nerves. The consultant does not sign and has never worked with a Deaf client. The consultant cannot find a signing consultant, including by telehealth, and Nia prefers to work with this consultant. What is the most appropriate way to proceed?
options: Use typed chat on a shared screen during sessions, and add notes she can review afterward
With Nia's agreement, have a teammate fluent in ASL interpret under a confidentiality pledge
Refer Nia to campus counseling staff who have experience working with Deaf students
Arrange a qualified ASL interpreter, and seek consultation on Deaf culture as the work begins
rationales: Written English may not be Nia's first language, and typing slows and flattens the conversation; it shifts the burden of the communication gap onto her.
A teammate has a dual relationship with Nia and is not a trained interpreter, which compromises both confidentiality and accuracy even with her agreement.
Pre-match nerves are a performance concern within the consultant's scope, and she has chosen this consultant; referring her to counseling because she is Deaf mismatches the service to the need.

Best. When no specialist is available and the client prefers the consultant, competence is extended responsibly by using a qualified, confidentiality-bound interpreter (often arranged through campus disability services) and seeking consultation and education on Deaf culture and interpreter-mediated work.
takeaway: Extend competence through qualified supports and consultation rather than declining or improvising.

stem: While consulting with a collegiate football program, a consultant hears position coaches praise players who 'play hurt' and joke that players in the athletic training room are 'soft.' Two players have told the consultant in confidence that they hide minor injuries to keep their spots. The consultant's contract is with the athletic department. Which action best fulfills the consultant's professional responsibilities?
options: Teach the two players pain-coping skills, and encourage them to see the athletic trainer when ready
Tell the athletic trainer which players are hiding injuries, and brief the head coach on the pattern
Urge both players to get evaluated, and raise the pattern with leadership without naming either
Encourage both players to see the athletic trainer, and leave coaching culture to the coaching staff
rationales: Pain-coping skills are an adjunct to medical care, not a substitute; teaching them while evaluation waits helps athletes keep playing on hidden injuries.
Naming the players breaks confidences shared about minor injuries with no imminent danger, and briefing the head coach routes the concern back through the group that created the pressure.

Best. Concern for others' welfare calls for getting the hidden injuries evaluated by sports medicine and for addressing the norm itself. Praising players who play hurt and stigmatizing the training room discourages injury reporting, so the pattern is raised with department leadership, the consultant's contracting party, framed around what the consultant observed without identifying the two players.

Getting the players evaluated is right, but concern for others' welfare and social responsibility extend to the organizational norm the consultant has observed, which will keep discouraging injury reporting.
takeaway: Sport norms that discourage reporting injuries are a welfare issue to address at the organizational level, protecting individual confidences.

stem: On a video call with Diego, a professional esports player born and raised in Texas, the consultant comments, 'Your English is really good.' At their next session, Diego says the remark bothered him because people often assume he is not American. What is the most appropriate response from the consultant?
options: Thank Diego for raising it, explain what the remark was meant to convey, and apologize for the hurt
Listen without defending, acknowledge the impact and the assumption behind it, and apologize
Apologize briefly, and return to performance topics so the session stays focused on Diego's goals
Apologize, and ask Diego how the consultant could avoid similar remarks with future clients
rationales: Explaining intent, even alongside an apology, centers the consultant and implicitly asks the client to discount the impact he just described.

Best. The remark is a microaggression that treats him as a foreigner in his own country. Repairing the rupture means non-defensive listening, acknowledging impact and the underlying assumption, and a sincere apology, followed by the consultant's own reflection.
A brief apology followed by a quick return to performance skips the repair the client invited and can signal that his concern is unwelcome.
Asking him to coach the consultant on future clients places the burden of education on the person who was harmed; that learning is the consultant's own responsibility.
takeaway: When told you caused harm, focus on impact over intent: listen, acknowledge, apologize, and reflect.

stem: Harper, a newly certified consultant who has worked only in collegiate athletics, takes a position with a professional baseball organization. In her first month she notices unwritten rules about who speaks in staff meetings, how players view staff who 'haven't played,' and how roster moves affect trust in the clubhouse. Which plan would best develop her contextual intelligence in this new setting?
options: Find a mentor among veteran staff, observe before intervening, and reflect on what she learns
Survey players and staff about their needs, and launch the programs they rate most highly
Ask the general manager to introduce her at a team meeting, then present her service menu
Study published research on professional baseball culture, and apply it to her service plan
rationales: Best. Contextual intelligence, the ability to read and work within an organization's culture, history, and power dynamics, develops through experience, mentoring, observation, and deliberate reflection.

A needs survey is useful input, but it cannot reveal the unwritten rules and trust dynamics she has noticed, and launching programs from ratings alone moves to intervention before she understands the setting.
A formal introduction gives visibility, but presenting services early relies on positional authority before she understands the clubhouse norms she has just begun to notice.
Published research describes the sport broadly, but contextual intelligence is about this organization's particular culture, relationships, and politics, which reading cannot supply.
takeaway: Contextual intelligence grows through mentoring, observation, and reflection in the new setting.

stem: After a widely shared incident in which a manager mocked an employee's accent, a technology company asks a consultant to deliver a one-hour diversity session for all staff next week. The consultant provides performance and team-development services and has no specific training in diversity education. An executive says the goal is 'to show we've dealt with it.' Which response best reflects the consultant's professional responsibilities?
options: Deliver the session next week, and tell leadership in advance that it is a first step, not a fix
Explain what one session can achieve, and recommend sustained work led by a DEI specialist
Agree to the session, and co-facilitate it with an HR staff member who knows the incident well
Offer a one-hour team communication workshop instead, which fits the consultant's expertise
rationales: Being candid about limits is good, but delivering diversity education without training in it falls outside the consultant's competence, and a one-off session still serves the 'dealt with it' framing.

Best. Integrity requires honesty about what a single session can and cannot do, since climate change depends on leadership commitment, policy, and sustained work. Competence requires recognizing that this work exceeds the consultant's training, so recommending qualified DEI specialists, with the consultant supporting team-development pieces if useful, is the responsible response.
A co-facilitator who knows the incident does not supply the missing expertise, and agreeing to the one-off session still lends the consultant's name to a public-relations goal.
Staying within competence is right, but a substitute workshop on communication does not address the incident and can be presented as having 'dealt with it.'
takeaway: In organizational DEIB work, be honest about what a one-off session can achieve and push for sustained, leadership-backed change.

stem: Six weeks after ACL reconstruction, Liv, an elite alpine skier, tells the consultant, 'I'll never ski the way I did.' She has been skipping home exercises and has stopped attending team video sessions. Her physical therapist reports normal healing. Using the integrated model of psychological response to sport injury, how should the consultant interpret these data to guide the plan?
options: She is in an expected grief stage, so the plan should support her until she reaches acceptance
Her withdrawal reflects lost team contact, so the plan should restore that contact before other work
Her stress response raised her injury risk, so the plan should center on preventing a re-injury
Her appraisal of the injury is shaping her mood and adherence, so the plan should target it
rationales: Stage or grief models of injury response are poorly supported; responses do not follow a fixed sequence, and waiting for 'acceptance' would delay help with her adherence.

Social support is a situational factor in the model and matters here, but her own statement points to an appraisal driving both mood and behavior; reconnecting her first leaves that driver unaddressed.
The stress response and injury risk belong to the stress–injury model, which predicts who gets injured; it does not explain her reactions after injury.

Best. In Wiese-Bjornstal's integrated model, cognitive appraisals ('I'll never be the same') shape emotional and behavioral responses such as adherence and withdrawal, so the plan targets her appraisals and, given her withdrawal, her social support.
takeaway: In the integrated model, appraisals drive emotional and behavioral responses to injury, so they are a key intervention target.

stem: A ballet company's artistic director asks a consultant to help reduce injuries during its demanding audition and premiere season. Medical staff report that most injuries last season occurred among dancers who were relocating or facing contract uncertainty, and dancers describe intense worry and muscle tension before casting announcements. Based on the stress–injury model, which program component should the consultant prioritize?
options: Cognitive-behavioral stress management, offered first to the dancers carrying the most pressure
Pre-performance routines that steady dancers' focus during auditions and premiere performances
Motivational imagery of successful premieres to build dancers' confidence for the season ahead
Rehabilitation goal setting so that injured dancers stay committed to their recovery programs
rationales: Best. Andersen and Williams' model holds that history of stressors, personality, and coping resources shape the stress response (cognitive appraisal plus physiological and attentional changes), which raises injury risk. Cognitive-behavioral stress management targets both the appraisal and the physical and attentional responses, and prioritizing dancers under the heaviest life stress follows the model's risk factors.
Routines can steady focus in the moment of performance, but they do not address the life stress, threat appraisals, and chronic tension the model links to injury across the season.
Building confidence and drive does little to reduce the threat appraisals and tension the model links to injury, and added arousal may intensify the stress response.
Rehab goal setting is useful after injury, but the request is to reduce injuries, which the model addresses before injury occurs.
takeaway: The stress–injury model points prevention at the stress response, appraisals plus physical and attentional changes, especially for athletes under heavy life stress.

stem: Curtis, a firefighter recovering from shoulder surgery, has been inconsistent with his prescribed home exercises and keeps asking his physical therapist when he can return to duty. He says the long rehab timeline feels 'like a black hole.' With his consent, the consultant and physical therapist are developing his plan together. Which goal-setting approach best fits this situation?
options: Agree on a return-to-duty date with the therapist, and plan weekly steps backward from that date
Break his protocol into weekly milestone goals, and review progress on them with the therapist
Set fitness goals for his uninjured areas, and leave goals for the shoulder to the therapist
Set longer-term career goals for after his return, so the rehab work has a clear purpose
rationales: A return date is an outcome goal controlled by healing and medical clearance; anchoring the plan to it invites discouragement if it slips and can pressure an early return.

Best. Short-term, specific process goals tied to protocol milestones break a long timeline into achievable steps, and shared review with the therapist supports adherence and keeps goals aligned with the medical plan.
Maintaining fitness elsewhere can help mood, but it sidesteps the home exercises he is skipping, which is the adherence problem the joint plan is meant to solve.
Distant career goals add purpose but do nothing to break up the 'black hole' of the timeline into near-term steps he can see himself completing.
takeaway: In rehab, short-term process goals tied to the medical protocol improve adherence more than a distant return date.

topic: Working with athletic trainers and consent
stem: An athletic trainer tells the consultant that Odessa, a collegiate lacrosse player recovering from a shoulder dislocation, often skips the last sets of her rehab exercises and seems discouraged. The trainer asks the consultant to 'work with her on it' and to share what they discuss. Odessa has agreed to meet with the consultant but has not yet done so. What should the consultant do first?
options: Review Odessa's rehab notes with the trainer, so the first session can focus on the skipped sets
Agree to give the trainer brief progress updates, and schedule a first session with Odessa
Meet Odessa, explain the consultant's role, and agree with her on what the trainer will be told
Hold a joint meeting with Odessa and the trainer to set rehab goals and decide what will be shared
rationales: Reviewing her records with the trainer before she has consented to the consultant's involvement or to any exchange of information bypasses her consent.
Promising updates to the trainer decides what will be shared before Odessa has had any say, which reverses the order informed consent requires.

Best. A third-party referral starts with meeting the athlete, explaining the consultant's role, and obtaining her informed consent, including exactly what will and will not be shared with the athletic trainer. Coordination follows from that agreement.
Joint planning may follow, but deciding what will be shared with the trainer in the room makes it hard for Odessa to choose freely; consent about disclosure is set with her first.
takeaway: Interdisciplinary teamwork runs on the athlete's informed consent; get it before sharing anything.

stem: Gloria, a 58-year-old triathlete, is four weeks into physical therapy after knee surgery. She tells the consultant that her stretching exercises are painful, that she tenses up and holds her breath during them, and that she has started skipping them at home. Her physical therapist has said some discomfort is expected. How should the consultant help Gloria during this phase?
options: Teach paced breathing and attention strategies, and have her report sharp pain to the therapist
Teach distraction techniques to help her push through each stretch, and review progress weekly
Ask the therapist whether the stretches can be eased, and add relaxation once they feel manageable
Link each stretch to her return-to-race goals, and track her home adherence with a daily log
rationales: Best. Relaxation and attentional strategies are evidence-based adjuncts that reduce tension and help athletes tolerate expected rehab discomfort, and breathing directly targets the breath-holding she describes, while the physical therapist remains the judge of which pain signals a problem.
Distraction can help with discomfort, but framing it as pushing through every stretch leaves out any check on sharp pain and does not address her tensing and breath-holding.
Her therapist has already said the discomfort is expected; asking for easier stretches second-guesses the prescription, and delaying coping skills leaves her without help now.
Linking stretches to goals and logging adherence may help motivation, but neither addresses the tension and breath-holding that are making the stretches hard to tolerate.
takeaway: Mental skills help athletes cope with expected rehab discomfort; the medical team decides what pain means and what to change.

stem: During a mental skills session, Ronan, a 16-year-old on his high school hockey team, mentions that he has had headaches, trouble concentrating, and sensitivity to light since taking a hard hit two days ago. He has not told the team's athletic trainer because Friday's playoff game is important and he does not want to be held out. He asks the consultant to keep this between them. What should the consultant do?
options: Encourage Ronan to tell the trainer himself before Friday, and check with him tomorrow that he did
Explain the risks of playing with these symptoms, and leave the decision about reporting to him
Call his parents tonight about the symptoms, and let them decide whether to involve the trainer
Explain that the symptoms need medical evaluation, and make sure the trainer hears about them today
rationales: Encouraging self-report is a good instinct, but leaving it to a minor who wants to play, and checking only tomorrow, delays evaluation of a possible concussion that should happen now.

Education matters, but whether a possible concussion is reported is not his choice alone: it is a safety limit on confidentiality, and leaving it to a minor who wants to play exposes him to further injury.

Parents should be involved, but routing the decision through them delays medical evaluation and leaves whether the medical team is told to chance; the athletic trainer's protocol will bring parents in.

Best. Concussion assessment and return-to-play decisions belong to the medical team. Explaining why, and ideally informing the athletic trainer together with Ronan, protects his safety and respects the safety limits of confidentiality set out at consent; the trainer's protocol will also involve his parents.
takeaway: Suspected concussion goes to the medical team immediately; it is a safety limit on confidentiality.

stem: Bianca, a collegiate volleyball setter, is three months into rehab for a torn Achilles tendon. Her rehab sessions are scheduled during team practice, and she tells the consultant she feels 'invisible' and disconnected from her teammates. She gives the consultant permission to talk with her coach about this. Which strategy should the consultant suggest to the coach?
options: Give her time away from team activities to focus on rehab, and plan a welcome-back for her return
Give her a meaningful team role, such as charting opponents, and include her in team meetings
Ask teammates to send her regular messages, and share her rehab progress at team meetings
Ask the athletic trainer to move her rehab outside practice, so she can watch practice with the team
rationales: Time away deepens the isolation she describes, which is a known risk to mood and adherence during long rehab; a welcome-back months later does not help now.

Best. Injured athletes often lose belonging and identity when separated from the team. A meaningful role and inclusion in team activities supply social support and keep her connected, which supports adjustment and recovery.
Messages are a kind gesture but keep her outside team activities, and sharing her medical progress with the team goes beyond what she agreed to.
Rehab scheduling is the athletic trainer's call, and watching from the side would still leave her without a role, which is the core of feeling 'invisible.'
takeaway: Keep injured athletes connected to the team through meaningful roles; isolation undermines recovery.

stem: Yuna, an elite figure skater recovering from an ankle fracture, has been using healing imagery that the consultant introduced and says she enjoys it. Her physical therapist reports that she has missed two appointments, and Yuna explains that she believes the imagery is 'doing the healing,' so the exercises matter less. What is the most appropriate response from the consultant?
options: Pause the healing imagery, and set attendance goals for her physical therapy appointments
Ask her physical therapist to explain why the exercises remain essential to her recovery
Clarify that imagery supports rather than replaces rehab, and pair it with her therapy sessions
Keep the imagery as it is, and add a log so she can self-monitor her home exercises
rationales: The imagery itself is not the problem; her belief about what it does is. Pausing it drops a tool she values instead of correcting the misunderstanding.

The therapist's input helps, but the consultant introduced the imagery and is best placed to correct what Yuna believes it does; handing that off leaves the misunderstanding in place in their own sessions.

Best. Imagery and other mental skills are adjuncts to medical care. Correcting the misunderstanding and linking imagery to her rehab sessions (for example, practicing before exercises) supports adherence instead of competing with it.
Self-monitoring can aid adherence, but leaving the imagery unchanged leaves intact the belief that led her to skip treatment.
takeaway: Imagery supports rehabilitation but never replaces prescribed medical care.

stem: Nine months after ACL reconstruction, Samuel, a professional soccer midfielder, has been medically cleared to return. In reassessment sessions he reports vivid worries about re-tearing the ligament, and he avoids tackles and sharp cuts in training. The head coach asks the consultant whether Samuel is 'ready to play.' Samuel has agreed that the consultant can share general progress with the coach. How should the consultant respond?
options: Explain that clearance and readiness can differ, and describe the ongoing work on his confidence
Recommend a gradual build-up of his match minutes, and explain how it would ease his worries
Share his re-injury anxiety scores, and let the coach weigh them when making selection decisions
Explain that readiness to play is the medical team's call, and direct the coach to them instead
rationales: Best. Physical clearance and psychological readiness are distinct: re-injury anxiety and avoidance can persist after medical clearance. Within the consent Samuel gave, the consultant can describe this in general terms and the continuing work on confidence, while return-to-play and selection decisions stay with the medical team and coach.
Recommending how many minutes he plays steps into selection, which is the coach's decision, even if the reasoning about his worries is sound.
Specific scores go beyond the general progress Samuel agreed to share, and inviting their use in selection turns assessment data into a basis for decisions he did not consent to.
Medical clearance is the medical team's call, but the coach is asking about more than clearance; declining to describe the psychological picture Samuel agreed to share withholds useful context.
takeaway: Medical clearance does not equal psychological readiness; communicate within consent and leave clearance decisions to the medical team.

topic: Recognizing a clinical concern in rehab
stem: At a scheduled progress review three months into rehabilitation for a back injury, Carmen, a collegiate gymnast, says that for several weeks she has felt hopeless nearly every day, sleeps poorly, has lost interest in friends and classes, and 'can't see the point anymore.' When asked directly, she denies any thoughts of harming herself and any plan to do so. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Explain that low mood is common in long rehabs, and add goals to restore her sense of progress
Add daily mood tracking to her plan, and review the ratings together at each weekly session
Share the concern with her athletic trainer, and ask the medical team to decide on next steps
Discuss a referral to a licensed mental health professional, and help her make the connection
rationales: Some low mood is common in rehab, but weeks of near-daily hopelessness, poor sleep, and loss of interest go beyond it; normalizing and adding goals delays care for a possible clinical concern.
Monitoring has value, but tracking mood within the performance plan does not get her assessed or treated for symptoms that suggest a possible mood disorder.
Coordinating with the medical team may be part of the response, but sharing before discussing it with Carmen bypasses her consent, and the referral conversation should start with her.

Best. Weeks of near-daily hopelessness, disrupted sleep, and loss of interest go beyond a typical injury response and suggest a clinical concern outside CMPC scope. A referral with a warm handoff gets her appropriate care, and performance support can continue alongside it; because she 'can't see the point,' the consultant should also keep checking on risk and know the crisis resources to use if it changes.
takeaway: When injury response looks like a clinical concern, refer to a licensed professional; reserve emergency steps for imminent risk.

topic: Revising rehab goals after a setback
stem: Rodrigo, an elite wheelchair basketball player, had been meeting his weekly rehab goals after shoulder surgery. At a progress review, he reports that a post-surgical complication has led his surgeon to extend his rehab timeline by eight weeks, and he says his goals 'feel pointless now.' What should the consultant do next?
options: Keep his current weekly goals, and add an outcome goal tied to the surgeon's new return date
Review the gains he has made so far, and reset his short-term goals to the revised timeline
Pause goal setting for a few weeks, and focus sessions on helping him work through his frustration
Shift his goals to conditioning his uninjured areas, and return to rehab goals once he is cleared
rationales: His weekly goals were built for the old timeline, and adding a distant outcome date does not make them attainable again.

Best. Evaluation includes revising goals when circumstances change. Reviewing progress already made and recalibrating short-term goals to the medical team's new timeline restores attainable targets and a sense of control.
Acknowledging his frustration matters, but pausing goals for weeks removes the structure that was working and leaves him without a sense of progress.
Conditioning goals can supplement rehab, but moving away from rehab goals abandons the area where attainable targets would most restore his sense of control.
takeaway: After a rehab setback, revise goals to the new timeline and highlight progress already made.

stem: Rin, a professional esports player with chronic wrist pain, tells the consultant during a virtual session that her hand surgeon has offered either surgery or a longer course of conservative treatment. She says she feels overwhelmed and does not know how to think the choice through, then asks, 'You know me best, so which should I choose?' She has an important tournament in three months. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Talk through each option against her tournament timeline, and share which one seems the better fit
Explain that this is outside the consultant's scope, and encourage her to raise it with her surgeon
Help her sort out her priorities and questions for the surgeon, without recommending an option
Describe how other players the consultant has worked with fared after each type of treatment
rationales: Weighing the options against her schedule is reasonable thinking, but offering a view on which treatment fits better is medical advice outside CMPC competence.
Naming the scope limit is correct, but stopping there leaves an overwhelmed client alone with a decision the consultant can help her think through.

Best. Practicing within competence means not advising on medical treatment, but the consultant can still help: clarifying her values, concerns, and questions supports an informed decision made with her surgeon.
Other clients' outcomes are anecdotes that may not apply to her condition, and sharing them steers a medical choice while risking others' confidentiality.
takeaway: Don't make medical recommendations; help the athlete prepare for an informed conversation with the medical team.

stem: At a weekly sports medicine meeting, a physical therapist asks the consultant to describe what Ayesha, an injured collegiate soccer player, has said in sessions about her fears and her family situation. Ayesha signed a release allowing the consultant to share her mental skills plan and attendance with the medical staff. How should the consultant respond?
options: Share the plan and attendance she authorized, and offer to ask Ayesha whether she wants more shared
Share the plan and attendance, and add a brief summary of her fears, since they bear on her rehab
Suggest the therapist ask Ayesha directly, and hold off on sharing anything until she has been asked
Share the requested details with the care team, and document that they were shared in a clinical meeting
rationales: Best. Disclosure is limited to what the client has authorized. The release covers her plan and attendance, so other content stays confidential unless a safety exception applies, and the consultant can ask Ayesha whether she wants more shared.
Relevance to rehab does not authorize disclosure; even a brief summary of her fears goes beyond what she agreed to release.
Checking with Ayesha is respectful, but she has already signed a release, and withholding what it covers undercuts the coordination she agreed to.
Documenting a disclosure does not make it authorized; team membership does not override the scope of her release.
takeaway: In interdisciplinary teams, share exactly what the athlete has authorized, no more and no less.

topic: Evidence on stage models of injury
stem: A consultant is preparing an evidence summary for athletic trainers who often describe injured athletes as moving through fixed stages, such as denial, anger, and acceptance. Which statement best reflects current research on psychological responses to sport injury?
options: Stage models capture the usual reactions well, although their order and timing vary by athlete
Stage models fit severe injuries reasonably well, but they apply less to minor, brief injuries
Fixed stages are poorly supported, and responses reflect how athletes appraise the injury in context
Fixed stages are poorly supported, and responses are best predicted by injury severity and recovery time
rationales: Allowing for variable order and timing still assumes a common set of stages, which research has not supported.
Stage models are not well supported for severe injuries either; the limitation is not about severity.

Best. Reviews of injury-response models found little support for fixed grief-like stages; responses are better explained by cognitive appraisal models, in which personal and situational factors shape appraisals, emotions, and behaviors.

Rejecting stage models is correct, but severity and recovery time are only part of the picture; appraisal models show that how the athlete interprets the injury shapes emotional responses beyond severity.
takeaway: Stage/grief models of injury response are poorly supported; appraisal-based models fit the evidence better.
